latin: Tunc igitur etiam ipse sermo speciem et ornatum suum sumit, sonum et vocem, cum dicit deus, Fiat lux. haec est nativitas perfecta sermonis, dum ex deo procedit; conditus ab eo primum ad cogitatum in nomine sophiae—Dominus condidit me initium viarum; dehinc generatus ad effectum—Cum pararet caelum aderam illi; exinde eum patrem sibi faciens de quo procedendo filius factus est primogenitus, ut ante omnia genitus, et unigenitus, ut solus ex deo genitus, proprie de vulva cordis ipsius secundum quod et pater ipse testatur, Eructavit cor meum sermonem optimum;
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com text (no edition named on the page; copied exactly from it); read against Oehler 1853 scan, PDF p.262-263 (OCR)
english: Then, therefore, does the Word also Himself assume His own form and glorious garb, His own sound and vocal utterance, when God says, Let there be light. This is the perfect nativity of the Word, when He proceeds forth from God — formed by Him first to devise and think out all things under the name of Wisdom — The Lord created or formed me as the beginning of His ways; then afterward begotten, to carry all into effect — When He prepared the heaven, I was present with Him. Thus does He make Him equal to Him: for by proceeding from Himself He became His first-begotten Son, because begotten before all things; and His only-begotten also, because alone begotten of God, in a way peculiar to Himself, from the womb of His own heart — even as the Father Himself testifies: My heart, says He, has emitted my most excellent Word.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, Roberts/Donaldson; text as on newadvent.org, Scripture-reference lines removed)
page: English: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers; Latin: Oehler printed pp.242-243 (PDF p.262-263; OCR, p.243 header OCR-read)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Scribner 1918 scan on archive.org, antenicenefather03robe; English text read from newadvent.org)
what_it_says: The Word becomes a perfect "nativity" when He proceeds from God: first conceived as Wisdom to plan, then begotten to carry out.
use: answer to objection (Prov. 8:22 "created/formed" read as creation, not generation)
limits: Proverbs 8:22 is read here as the Word's own procession; the passage does not state an eternal begetting, and "ante omnia genitus" sits next to a sequence of stages.

latin: in qua effigie dei? utique in aliqua, non tamen in nulla: quis enim negabit deum corpus esse, etsi deus spiritus est? spiritus enim corpus sui generis in sua effigie.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com text (no edition named on the page; copied exactly from it); matches Oehler p.244 (image read)
english: In what form of God? Of course he means in some form, not in none. For who will deny that God is a body, although God is a Spirit? For Spirit has a bodily substance of its own kind, in its own form.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, Roberts/Donaldson; text as on newadvent.org, Scripture-reference lines removed)
page: English: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers; Latin: Oehler printed p.244 (PDF p.264, image read)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Scribner 1918 scan on archive.org, antenicenefather03robe; English text read from newadvent.org)
what_it_says: Tertullian says God is a body although God is spirit, because spirit is a body of its own kind in its own form.
use: objection (anti-Trinitarians and later critics cite it as divine corporealism)
limits: Tertullian qualifies it ("in some form, not in none"); Nicene theology excludes divine corporeality (see Athanasius, De Decretis 22, 24). The brief's wording "spiritus etiam corporis sui generis" is not in the text; the printed text is "spiritus enim corpus sui generis in sua effigie".

latin: sermo ergo et in patre semper, sicut dicit, Ego in patre: et apud deum semper, sicut scriptum est, Et sermo erat apud deum: et nunquam separatus a patre aut alias a patre quia Ego et pater unum sumus.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com text (no edition named on the page; copied exactly from it); matches Oehler p.245 (image read)
english: But the Word was formed by the Spirit, and (if I may so express myself) the Spirit is the body of the Word. The Word, therefore, is both always in the Father, as He says, I am in the Father; and is always with God, according to what is written, And the Word was with God; and never separate from the Father, or other than the Father, since I and the Father are one.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, Roberts/Donaldson; text as on newadvent.org, Scripture-reference lines removed)
page: English: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers; Latin: Oehler printed p.245 (PDF p.265, image read)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Scribner 1918 scan on archive.org, antenicenefather03robe; English text read from newadvent.org)
what_it_says: The Word is always in the Father and never separated from Him, since "I and the Father are one".
use: supports Trinitarian reading (unity of substance with distinction)
limits: Tertullian calls the Spirit "body" of the Word ("sermonis corpus est spiritus"), which is non-Nicene language; he uses "unum" without the later homoousios vocabulary.

latin: haec erit probolh_ veritatis, custos unitatis, qua prolatum dicimus filium a patre sed non separatum. protulit enim deus sermonem, quemadmodum etiam paracletus docet, sicut radix fruticem et fons fluvium et sol radium: nam et istae species probolhai\ sunt earum substantiarum ex quibus prodeunt. nec dubitaverim filium licere et radicis fruticem et fontis fluvium et solis radium, quia omnis origo parens est et omne quod ex origine profertur progenies est, multo magis sermo dei qui etiam proprie nomen filii accepit: nec frutex tamen a radice nec fluvius a fonte nec radius a sole discernitur, sicut nec a deo sermo.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com text (no edition named on the page; copied exactly from it); start on Oehler p.245 (image read); end (nec a deo sermo) is on printed p.246, which is not in this scan
english: This will be the prolation, taught by the truth, the guardian of the Unity, wherein we declare that the Son is a prolation from the Father, without being separated from Him. For God sent forth the Word, as the Paraclete also declares, just as the root puts forth the tree, and the fountain the river, and the sun the ray. For these are προβολαί, or emanations, of the substances from which they proceed. I should not hesitate, indeed, to call the tree the son or offspring of the root, and the river of the fountain, and the ray of the sun; because every original source is a parent, and everything which issues from the origin is an offspring. Much more is (this true of) the Word of God, who has actually received as His own peculiar designation the name of Son. But still the tree is not severed from the root, nor the river from the fountain, nor the ray from the sun; nor, indeed, is the Word separated from God.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, Roberts/Donaldson; text as on newadvent.org, Scripture-reference lines removed)
page: Oehler printed p.245 (PDF p.265) for the start; printed p.246 not located in the scan
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Scribner 1918 scan on archive.org, antenicenefather03robe; English text read from newadvent.org)
what_it_says: The Son is a prolation of the Father "without being separated", as root to tree, fountain to river, sun to ray; the Word is not separated from God.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (non-separation) but the analogies are Tertullian's own
limits: The images are partitive or emanative (the ray is a portion of the sun), and Tertullian himself says "probolē" is a Valentinian term; Athanasius rejects the sun-fire analogy (De Decretis 23). Printed p.246 not located in the scan.

latin: secundus autem ubi est, duo sunt, et tertius ubi est, tres sunt. tertius enim est spiritus a deo et filio, sicut tertius a radice fructus ex frutice et tertius a fonte rivus ex flamine et tertius a sole apex ex radio: nihil tamen a matrice alienatur a qua proprietates suas ducit. ita trinitas per consertos et connexos gradus a patre decurrens et monarchiae nihil obstrepit et oeconomiae statum protegit.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com text (no edition named on the page; copied exactly from it); printed p.246 not located in this scan, so no PDF page
english: Everything which proceeds from something else must needs be second to that from which it proceeds, without being on that account separated. Where, however, there is a second, there must be two; and where there is a third, there must be three. Now the Spirit indeed is third from God and the Son; just as the fruit of the tree is third from the root, or as the stream out of the river is third from the fountain, or as the apex of the ray is third from the sun. Nothing, however, is alien from that original source whence it derives its own properties. In like manner the Trinity, flowing down from the Father through intertwined and connected steps, does not at all disturb the Monarchy, while it at the same time guards the state of the Economy.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, Roberts/Donaldson; text as on newadvent.org, Scripture-reference lines removed)
page: page not located (printed p.246 is missing from the scan sequence)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Scribner 1918 scan on archive.org, antenicenefather03robe; English text read from newadvent.org)
what_it_says: The Father's order of the Trinity runs in linked steps (secundus, tertius) without disturbing the Monarchy or the Economy.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Monarchy kept, Economy distinguished) and answers the objection that "second" means a second God
limits: The "secundus/tertius" ordering language is what Arians cite for subordination; Tertullian uses it here to defend unity of origin, not equality of rank.

latin: non tamen diversitate alium filium a patre sed distributione, nec divisione alium sed distinctione, quia non sit idem pater et filius, vel modulo alias ab alio.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com text (no edition named on the page; copied exactly from it); printed p.246-247 not located in this scan
english: it is not by way of diversity that the Son differs from the Father, but by distribution: it is not by division that He is different, but by distinction; because the Father is not the same as the Son, since they differ one from the other in the mode of their being.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, Roberts/Donaldson; text as on newadvent.org, Scripture-reference lines removed)
page: page not located (printed pp.246-247 missing from the scan sequence)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Scribner 1918 scan on archive.org, antenicenefather03robe; English text read from newadvent.org)
what_it_says: The Son is other than the Father by distribution and distinction, not by diversity or division.
use: answer to objection (diversity read as separation)
limits: The sentence says "alium filium ... alium spiritum", which an objector reads as separate beings; Tertullian answers with distinctio/distributio, not with a Nicene formula.

latin: pater enim tota substantia est, filius vero, derivatio totius et portio, sicut ipse profitetur, Quia pater maior me est: a quo et minoratus canitur in psalmo, Modicum quid citra angelos.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com text (no edition named on the page; copied exactly from it); printed pp.246-247 not located in this scan; the printed order is "derivatio totius et portio"
english: For the Father is the entire substance, but the Son is a derivation and portion of the whole, as He Himself acknowledges: My Father is greater than I. In the Psalm His inferiority is described as being a little lower than the angels.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, Roberts/Donaldson; text as on newadvent.org, Scripture-reference lines removed)
page: page not located (printed pp.246-247 missing from the scan sequence)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Scribner 1918 scan on archive.org, antenicenefather03robe; English text read from newadvent.org)
what_it_says: The Father is the whole substance; the Son is a derivation and portion of the whole, and is "less" as begotten.
use: objection (anti-Trinitarians read "portio" as the Son being a part of God); answer via Hilary, De Trin. 2.6 and 2.8
limits: The brief's phrase "portio totius" does not occur; the text reads "derivatio totius et portio". Hilary (De Trin. 2.8) denies that the Son is a portion, so the two authors use the word with opposite implications.

latin: iam ergo alius erit qui videbatur, quia non potest idem invisibilis definiri qui videbatur: et consequens erit ut invisibilem patrem intellegamus pro plenitudine maiestatis, visibilem vero filium agnoscamus pro modulo derivationis, sicut nec solem nobis contemplari licet quantum ad ipsam substantiae summam quae est in caelis, radium autem eius toleramus oculis pro temperatura portionis quae in terram inde porrigitur.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com text (no edition named on the page; copied exactly from it); read against Oehler printed pp.255-256 (OCR)
english: It will therefore follow, that by Him who is invisible we must understand the Father in the fullness of His majesty, while we recognise the Son as visible by reason of the dispensation of His derived existence; even as it is not permitted us to contemplate the sun, in the full amount of his substance which is in the heavens, but we can only endure with our eyes a ray, by reason of the tempered condition of this portion which is projected from him to the earth.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, Roberts/Donaldson; text as on newadvent.org, Scripture-reference lines removed)
page: English: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers; Latin: Oehler printed pp.255-256 (PDF p.273-274, OCR)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Scribner 1918 scan on archive.org, antenicenefather03robe; English text read from newadvent.org)
what_it_says: The Father is invisible in the fullness of His majesty, while the Son is visible as the derivation of His existence, as the ray is seen where the sun is not.
use: answer to objection (invisibility of the Father in Exodus 33; Son as visible)
limits: The visible/invisible contrast is for theophanies; the sun-ray comparison makes the visibility of the Son partial, which Nicene theology does not use.

latin: Et cum radius ex sole porrigitur, portio ex summa; sed sol erit in radio, quia solis est radius nec separatur substantia sed extenditur, [ita de spiritu spiritus et de deo deus] ut lumen de lumine accensum. Manet integra et indefecta materia[e] matrix, etsi plures inde traduces qualitatis mutueris.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com text (no edition named on the page; copied exactly from it). Oehler p.94 (PDF 132) read from the rendered image has no brackets around "ita de spiritu spiritus et de deo deus"; "materiae" in Oehler (thelatinlibrary: "materia[e]")
english: Even when the ray is shot from the sun, it is still part of the parent mass; the sun will still be in the ray, because it is a ray of the sun — there is no division of substance, but merely an extension. Thus Christ is Spirit of Spirit, and God of God, as light of light is kindled. The material matrix remains entire and unimpaired, though you derive from it any number of shoots possessed of its qualities; so, too, that which has come forth out of God is at once God and the Son of God, and the two are one.
translator: S. Thelwall (ANF vol. 3; text as on newadvent.org)
page: Oehler printed p.94 (Apologeticum), read from the image; English: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Scribner 1918 scan on archive.org, antenicenefather03robe; English text read from newadvent.org)
what_it_says: The ray comes from the sun with no division of substance but an extension, and so the Son is "light of light" with God as "God of God".
use: supports Trinitarian reading (no division of substance); answers the portio objection by the sun-ray image
limits: Partitive wording ("portio ex summa") and the material matrix image; Athanasius (De Decretis 23) rejects the fire-from-sun analogy. The brief's phrase "non ... separatur sed excipitur" does not occur; the text reads "nec separatur substantia sed extenditur".

latin: Ita et quod de deo profectum est, deus et dei filius et unus ambo; ita et de spiritu spiritus et de deo deus modulo alter[num], numerum gradu, non statu fecit, et a matrice non recessit, sed excessit.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com text (no edition named on the page; copied exactly from it); Oehler p.95 (PDF 133) header and text read by OCR
english: In this way also, as He is Spirit of Spirit and God of God, He is made a second in manner of existence — in position, not in nature; and He did not withdraw from the original source, but went forth.
translator: S. Thelwall (ANF vol. 3; text as on newadvent.org)
page: Oehler printed pp.94-95 (PDF 132-133); p.95 header "APOLOGETICUS ADVERSUS GENTES. 95" read by OCR; English: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Scribner 1918 scan on archive.org, antenicenefather03robe; English text read from newadvent.org)
what_it_says: The Son, as Spirit of Spirit and God of God, is a second in manner of existence but not in nature, and did not withdraw from the original source but went forth.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (procession without separation: "non recessit, sed excessit")
limits: The brief's "a matrice ... separatur sed excipitur" is not in the text; the printed words are "a matrice non recessit, sed excessit". "Excessit" = went forth; the material matrix image is not Nicene.

latin: Nihil enim, si non corpus; incorporalitas enim ab omni genere custodiae libera est, immunis et a poena et a fouella. Per quod enim punitur aut fouetur, hoc erit corpus;
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com text (no edition named on the page; copied exactly from it); read against Oehler printed p.337 (PDF 355, image read)
english: For nothing it certainly is, if it is not a bodily substance. For whatever is incorporeal is incapable of being kept and guarded in any way; it is also exempt from either punishment or refreshment.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, Roberts/Donaldson; text as on newadvent.org, Scripture-reference lines removed)
page: Oehler printed p.337 (PDF p.355, image read); English: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Scribner 1918 scan on archive.org, antenicenefather03robe; English text read from newadvent.org)
what_it_says: If the soul were not body it could not be punished or refreshed: "Nothing, if not body" (nihil, si non corpus).
use: objection (Tertullian's corporealism, used by critics to argue he thought of spirit as body)
limits: About the soul, not God. Textual variants: Oehler reads "si nihil anima detinet sub terris" and "a fovela" where thelatinlibrary has "si nthil anima sub terris" (a typo) and "a fouella".

latin: Denique Zeno consitum spiritum definiens animam hoc modo instruit. Quo, inquit, digresso animal emoritur, corpus est; consito autem spiritu digresso animal emoritur, ergo consitus spiritus corpus est; ergo corpus est anima.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com text (no edition named on the page; copied exactly from it); Oehler PDF p.352 (image read; printed number not legible on the scan)
english: Indeed, Zeno, defining the soul to be a spirit generated with (the body,) constructs his argument in this way: That substance which by its departure causes the living being to die is a corporeal one. Now it is by the departure of the spirit, which is generated with (the body,) that the living being dies; therefore the spirit which is generated with (the body) is a corporeal substance. But this spirit which is generated with (the body) is the soul: it follows, then, that the soul is a corporeal substance.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, Roberts/Donaldson; text as on newadvent.org, Scripture-reference lines removed)
page: page unknown (printed number not legible on the scan header of PDF p.352)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Scribner 1918 scan on archive.org, antenicenefather03robe; English text read from newadvent.org)
what_it_says: Tertullian reports Zeno's Stoic argument that the departing spirit is a body, so the soul is a body.
use: context (shows Tertullian's Stoic source for corporealism)
limits: Reported as the argument of the Stoics in the chapter "Probable view of the Stoics"; not a clear statement of Tertullian's own view about God.

english: Accordingly, they wrote 'from the essence of God,' in order that 'from God?' might not be considered common and equal in the Son and in things originate, but that all others might be acknowledged as creatures, and the Word alone as from the Father.
translator: John Henry Newman (NPNF2 vol. 4)
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: NPNF2 vol. 4 (1892, Christian Literature Publishing Co.)
what_it_says: The Council wrote "from the essence of God" so that the Son is not counted with creatures as merely "from God".
use: supports Trinitarian reading (proper essence, not creation)
limits: Only the English was read. The Greek/Latin of Athanasius was not checked, and the brief's clause "ex substantia Patris" was not verified in any Latin text.

english: for never was the Word not, but He was always, existing everlastingly with the Father, as the radiance of light)
translator: John Henry Newman (NPNF2 vol. 4)
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: NPNF2 vol. 4 (1892)
what_it_says: The Word "never was not": He was always, existing everlastingly with the Father "as the radiance of light".
use: answer to objection (time when the Son was not)
limits: English only; the Greek was not read.

english: Again, the illustration of the Light and the Radiance has this meaning. For the Saints have not said that the Word was related to God as fire kindled from the heat of the sun, which is commonly put out again, for this is an external work and a creature of its author, but they all preach of Him as Radiance, thereby to signify His being from the essence, proper and indivisible, and His oneness with the Father.
translator: John Henry Newman (NPNF2 vol. 4)
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: NPNF2 vol. 4 (1892)
what_it_says: Athanasius rejects the image of fire kindled by the sun's heat as an external work; "radiance" signifies the Son's being from the essence.
use: limit on Tertullian's sun-ray analogy (Prax. 8.5, Apol. 21.12)
limits: Athanasius keeps the radiance image in a qualified sense; the analogy is not dropped.

english: Further, let every corporeal reference be banished on this subject; and transcending every imagination of sense, let us, with pure understanding and with mind alone, apprehend the genuine relation of son to father, and the Word's proper relation towards God, and the unvarying likeness of the radiance towards the light:
translator: John Henry Newman (NPNF2 vol. 4)
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: NPNF2 vol. 4 (1892)
what_it_says: Every corporeal reference should be banished from the doctrine; the Son is apprehended by pure understanding and mind alone.
use: limit on Tertullian's corporealism (Prax. 7.8)
limits: Athanasius does not name Tertullian; the instruction is a general rule.

english: If there never was, when the Son was not,' say they, 'but He is eternal, and coexists with the Father, you call Him no more the Father's Son, but brother.
translator: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson (NPNF2 vol. 4)
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: NPNF2 vol. 4 (1892)
what_it_says: The Arians object: if there was never when the Son was not, then the Son is a brother, not a Son.
use: objection (the Arian dilemma about the Son as "Son" vs "brother")
limits: The Arian formula is quoted as their objection; Athanasius's answer follows in 1.14-15.

english: they deny that the Son is the proper offspring of the Father's essence, on the ground that this must imply parts and divisions
translator: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson (NPNF2 vol. 4)
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: NPNF2 vol. 4 (1892)
what_it_says: Arians deny the Son is the proper offspring of the Father's essence on the ground that this would imply parts and divisions.
use: objection (this is the same worry the portio passages raise)
limits: Shows the Arian objection; Athanasius's answer about the undivided essence is in 1.16.

english: is it not blasphemous, God being Maker, to say, that His Framing Word and His Wisdom once was not?
translator: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson (NPNF2 vol. 4)
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: NPNF2 vol. 4 (1892)
what_it_says: If God creates through the Word, to say the Word once was not is blasphemous, since God is Maker.
use: answer to objection (creation through the Word implies an eternal Word)
limits: Argument from creation; it does not address Prov. 8:22 directly.

english: If then there is another Word of God, then be the Son originated by a word; but if there be not, as is the case, but all things by Him have come to be, which the Father has willed, does not this expose the many-headed craftiness of these men?
translator: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson (NPNF2 vol. 4)
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: NPNF2 vol. 4 (1892)
what_it_says: Athanasius turns the Arian argument back on them: all things came to be through the Son, so the Son cannot be made by another word.
use: answer to objection ("by will" / creature)
limits: Only 3.62 was read in full; 3.58-61 and 3.63 were not read as a set.

work: Symbolum Nicaenum (Latin; no council or version stated on the page)
latin: Deum de Deo, Lumen de Lumine, Deum verum de Deo vero, genitum non factum, consubstantialem Patri; per quem omnia facta sunt.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com/creeds.html, section "Symbolum Nicaenum" (no edition named); brief's "ex substantia Patris" not found
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: not obtained
what_it_says: The Latin creed calls the Son God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten not made, consubstantial with the Father.
use: answer (divinity and consubstantiality)
limits: English not obtained. "ex substantia Patris" is not in this Latin text; the 325 Greek "ek tēs ousias" appears only in Athanasius (De Decretis 19, in English).

english: For it is said in relation to something, as the Father in relation to the Son and the Son in relation to the Father, which is not accident;
translator: Arthur West Haddan (NPNF1 vol. 3)
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: NPNF1 vol. 3 (1887)
what_it_says: The Father and Son are said in relation to each other, and this is not an accident in God because God does not change.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (relation without change)
limits: Latin not obtained; "part" is not discussed here.

english: Some think themselves hindered from admitting the equality of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because it is written, Christ, the power of God, and the wisdom of God; in that, on this ground, there does not appear to be equality; because the Father is not Himself power and wisdom, but the begetter of power and wisdom.
translator: Arthur West Haddan (NPNF1 vol. 3)
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: NPNF1 vol. 3 (1887)
what_it_says: Some hold that the Father is not Himself power and wisdom, so the equality of the Son is denied; Augustine takes up the question.
use: context (the Arian objection to equality)
limits: Negative result: the word "part" in De Trinitate V-VI occurs only in the discussion of bodies, not of the Son's relation to the Father. Only the opening paragraph was read.

english: Some have understood it in the sense of an effect, proceeding from its cause; so Arius took it, saying that the Son proceeds from the Father as His primary creature, and that the Holy Ghost proceeds from the Father and the Son as the creature of both.
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (newadvent.org)
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: Summa Theologiae (English Dominican Province translation, as on newadvent.org)
what_it_says: Arius takes the Son's procession as an effect, making the Son a primary creature; Thomas rejects that reading.
use: answer to objection (Arian procession as creature)
limits: Latin not obtained: corpusthomisticum.org now redirects to 404; the Latin was not recovered.

english: for this kind of generation requires that there should be a procession by way of similitude in the same specific nature; as a man proceeds from a man, and a horse from a horse.
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (newadvent.org)
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: Summa Theologiae (English Dominican Province translation, as on newadvent.org)
what_it_says: The Word's procession is called generation because it is by way of likeness in the same nature, as a man proceeds from a man.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (generation means procession by likeness in one nature)
limits: Analogy from living things; "portion" is not addressed. Latin not obtained.

english: In God relation is not a universal whole, although it is predicated of each of the relations; because all the relations are one in essence and being, which is irreconcilable with the idea of universal, the parts of which are distinguished in being. Persons likewise is not a universal term in God as we have seen above (I:30:4). Wherefore all the relations together are not greater than only one; nor are all the persons something greater than only one; because the whole perfection of the divine nature exists in each person.
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (newadvent.org)
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: Summa Theologiae (English Dominican Province translation, as on newadvent.org)
what_it_says: In God relation is not a universal whole; all the relations are one in essence, so the number of relations does not make the Son less than the Father.
use: answer to objection (whole and part in God)
limits: Addresses whole-and-part only in the sense of relations, not Tertullian's "portio". Latin not obtained.

english: The Son is necessarily equal to the Father in greatness. For the greatness of God is nothing but the perfection of His nature.
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (newadvent.org)
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: Summa Theologiae (English Dominican Province translation, as on newadvent.org)
what_it_says: The Son is necessarily equal to the Father in greatness, since the greatness of God is the perfection of His nature.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (equality of greatness)
limits: Latin not obtained. Q.33 a.2-3 were only checked by their titles and are not used.

english: For a part implies division, a whole is undivided, and God is everywhere and wholly present wherever He is.
translator: E.W. Watson and L. Pullan (NPNF2 vol. 9)
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: NPNF2 vol. 9 (1899)
what_it_says: For a part implies division, while a whole is undivided, and God is wholly present wherever He is.
use: answer to objection (divine wholeness, against "portio")
limits: Speaks of God as a whole, not specifically of the Son; Latin not checked.

english: Nor is there a portion of the Father resident in the Son, for the Son bears witness, All things that the Father has are Mine, and again, And all things that are Mine are Yours, and Yours are Mine, and the Apostle testifies, For in Him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily; and by the nature of things a portion cannot possess the whole.
translator: E.W. Watson and L. Pullan (NPNF2 vol. 9)
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: NPNF2 vol. 9 (1899)
what_it_says: There is no portion of the Father in the Son, because a portion cannot possess the whole.
use: answer to objection (rejects Tertullian-style "portio" as partition); compare Prax. 9.2
limits: Hilary denies "portion" outright, while Tertullian uses "portio" of the Son (Prax. 9.2) with derivation; Latin not checked, so the word "portio" in Hilary is unverified.

english: It is no rending or severance, for He that begot is without passions, and He that was born is the Image of the invisible God and bears witness, The Father is in Me and I in the Father.
translator: E.W. Watson and L. Pullan (NPNF2 vol. 9)
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: NPNF2 vol. 9 (1899)
what_it_says: The Son's birth is no rending or severance: the Begetter is without passions, and the Son is the Image of the invisible God.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (generation without division)
limits: Latin not checked.

english: He, then, when the Father willed it, proceeded from the Father, and He who was in the Father came forth from the Father; and He who was in the Father because He was of the Father, was subsequently with the Father, because He came forth from the Father — that is to say, that divine substance whose name is the Word, whereby all things were made, and without whom nothing was made.
translator: Robert Ernest Wallis (ANF vol. 5)
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: ANF vol. 5 (1886)
what_it_says: The Son proceeded from the Father when the Father willed it, and is the Word whereby all things were made.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Son as the Word through whom all was made); but see limits
limits: Novatian says the Son "has a beginning in that He is born" and proceeds "when the Father willed it": language that later Nicene theology (eternal generation) avoids. Latin not checked.

english: For if He had not been born — compared with Him who was unborn, an equality being manifested in both — He would make two unborn beings, and thus would make two Gods.
translator: Robert Ernest Wallis (ANF vol. 5)
page: newadvent text carries no printed page numbers
edition: ANF vol. 5 (1886)
what_it_says: If the Son were not born, He would be a second unborn being and so a second God; His birth keeps Him one God with the Father.
use: answer to objection (two-Gods argument)
limits: The argument depends on Novatian's own premise that the Father alone is unbegotten; Latin not checked.
